summary:
West Pomeranian Voivodeship stands under the national framework of Poland. Poland provides no hate-crime protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity; a March 2025 amendment bill that would introduce it was referred to the Constitutional Tribunal, where hearings were held in July and September 2025. Legal gender recognition remains court-based and medically gatekept. The anti-LGBT municipal-resolution wave, which covered more than 80 municipalities and four voivodeship-level declarations as of March 2020, concentrated in the eastern and south-eastern parts of the country, so the absence of local findings in West Pomeranian Voivodeship indicates thinner documentation rather than established safety.

Detention is the clearest documented risk to a trans visitor in Poland. In a case publicised by the Association for Legal Intervention on 13 March 2024, a regional court placed a transgender Vietnamese woman, on hormone therapy since 2018, in a guarded centre for male foreign nationals. The Border Guard refused to move or release her despite her identifying as a woman and warning that stopping her medication would harm her; the centre would not supply the medication and her therapy was interrupted for three months. Release came only after the legal-aid organisation intervened citing Polish law, court rulings and international standards, prompting the Border Guard Commander to order her out on the ground that continued detention there posed a serious health risk. The same case documented her history of violence and sexual assault, indicating that trans women held in these facilities may face both untreated care needs and vulnerable placement.

Courts have proved willing to intervene. On 11 July 2024 the European Court of Human Rights found that Polish prison authorities violated Article 8 of the Convention by denying a trans woman hormone replacement therapy while she was imprisoned, despite hormones having been prescribed to her for almost two years, and awarded EUR 8,000 in damages while rejecting the Article 3 claim. The ruling establishes that medication denial in Polish custody is litigable and winnable, though Poland operates no specialised trans prison section and placement decisions remain individual and unpredictable.

Entry itself is straightforward for many nationalities: Global Affairs Canada's travel advisory notes visa-free entry for tourists staying up to 90 days. The same advisory lists sexual orientation among reported motives for harassment in Poland, alongside physical appearance and foreigner status, and links general LGBTQ2+ travel guidance.

The wider legal environment is in transition. Human Rights Watch describes LGBT-rights reform under the Prime Minister Tusk government as slow and insufficient through 2024. Deputy Justice Minister Smiszek announced a hate-speech law extending protection to gender identity and sexual orientation; a March draft Penal Code amendment raising penalties for anti-LGBTI hate speech and violence cleared the Government Legislation Centre in May before approval was postponed, and a second bill followed in late October 2024. The Prosecutor General established a special response team with new guidelines for law enforcement.

Recognition of same-sex relationships has moved materially. In June 2024 Justice Minister Bodnar revoked the directive issued by his predecessor Ziobro that had blocked recognition of same-sex marriage certificates obtained abroad, and in September 2024 the European Court of Human Rights ruled that Poland's absence of partnership recognition leaves couples in an illegal vacuum contrary to their rights, calling for a recognition framework.
tangentialFactors:
The documented anti-LGBT resolution movement is geographically uneven. Its concentration in eastern and south-eastern Poland means a voivodeship in the north-west of the country carries no equivalent record of municipal hostility, but the same geography also means there is little local reporting to weigh. Silence in West Pomeranian Voivodeship should be read as an absence of evidence about local practice, not as evidence of local tolerance.

Both trans-specific remedies in the inventory were obtained through litigation rather than routine administration. The Vietnamese woman's release from a male-only guarded centre followed NGO intervention, and the prisoner's EUR 8,000 award followed proceedings at the European Court of Human Rights. A visitor who is detained should expect to need a lawyer or an advocacy organisation to secure placement or medication, not a facility's own procedures.

Harassment risk reported to travellers is not limited to gender identity. Global Affairs Canada lists sexual orientation, physical appearance and foreigner status together as reported motives, which places a visibly foreign trans visitor at the intersection of two of those categories.

Poland's position sits between neighbouring regimes in the region: entry rules are permissive and visa-free for many nationalities, while the substantive protections that would follow from the pending hate-speech legislation are not yet in force. The gap between easy entry and weak protection is the defining feature of the current environment.

Those questions are not sourced and should not be inferred from the visa-free entry note.
